what: A circuit breaker sits in front of a call to another service. When that service keeps failing, it stops calling for a while and answers fast with a fallback, then tests carefully before trusting it again.
like: Like the fuse box at home: when a circuit overloads, the switch trips so the whole house stays safe, and you flip it back once the fault is fixed.
why: Stops one sick dependency from tying up threads and dragging your whole service down
Gives the struggling service room to recover instead of a flood of retries
Users get a quick fallback answer instead of a long wait and an error

nodes.t: AI search service|asks many answer engines
Engine A|the provider that is down
Sliding window|failure rate of last N
Wait timer|then let a few probes in
Back-fill queue|re-run when engine is back

steps.d: Each call to Engine A gets a deadline. A slow answer counts as a failure, so threads are never stuck waiting forever.
While closed, every success, error and slow call goes into a sliding window, either the last N calls or the last N seconds.
Once enough calls are counted and the failure rate passes the threshold, the breaker opens. A wait timer starts.
While open, calls are rejected at once without touching Engine A. The service shows a cached or partial answer and saves the job for later.
When the timer ends, a small number of trial calls go through. If they succeed the breaker closes; if they fail it opens again.
Traffic flows normally and a worker drains the back-fill queue slowly, so the recovered engine is not hit by a sudden burst.

numbers.l: Resilience4j default failure rate that opens the breaker
Resilience4j default wait in open before half-open
Resilience4j default sliding window size, counted in calls
extra load when 5 layers each retry 3 times
Envoy default time a failing host is ejected

choices.d: Pick the failure rate that trips it and the window: count-based (last 100 calls) or time-based (last 30 seconds). Set a minimum number of calls so three errors at night do not trip it.
How long to stay open before probing. Defaults differ: Polly (.NET) waits 5 seconds, Resilience4j (Java) 60. Too short hammers a sick service; too long keeps users on the fallback.
Base them on the dependency's real latency, for example its p99.9 (the slowest 1 in 1,000 calls). Count slow calls as failures too.
Retry only safe (idempotent) calls, at one layer of the stack, with exponential backoff plus random jitter and a retry budget that caps retries.
Cap concurrent calls per dependency so one engine cannot use every thread. Decide the fallback: cached answer, another provider, partial result or a queued job.

instead.why: Protects your service from too many callers, not from a sick dependency
Make the call async so a slow provider just delays the queue
Park messages that keep failing for later inspection and replay
With outlier detection, ejects one bad host while others keep serving

breaks.d: Every layer retries, so a small blip becomes many times the normal load and the dependency cannot recover.
breaks.see: Request rate to the dependency jumps far above user traffic
breaks.fix: Retry at one layer only, add backoff with jitter and a retry budget

breaks.d: Timeouts are too long, so calls hang instead of failing and threads run out first.
breaks.see: Thread pool or connection pool full, p99 latency at the timeout value
breaks.fix: Shorter timeouts, count slow calls as failures, add a bulkhead

breaks.d: It opens and closes again and again on low or noisy traffic.
breaks.see: State change events every few seconds on the dashboard
breaks.fix: Raise the minimum number of calls, widen the window, longer wait

breaks.d: When the breaker closes, the whole back-fill hits the engine at once and knocks it over again.
breaks.see: Breaker reopens right after half-open succeeds
breaks.fix: Drain the back-fill queue at a capped rate with jitter

breaks.d: Users quietly get stale answers for hours and nobody notices.
breaks.see: Fallback rate climbing while error rate looks fine
breaks.fix: Alert on breaker state and fallback rate, not only on errors

say: Every call to an answer engine goes through a timeout and a circuit breaker per provider, so one engine being down never ties up our workers.
The breaker uses a sliding window with a minimum call count, opens above a failure rate threshold, and probes in half-open after a wait.
Retries happen at one layer only, with exponential backoff, full jitter and a retry budget, so we do not create a retry storm.
While Engine A is open we serve the other engines, mark its results as pending, and back-fill from a queue at a capped rate once it recovers.

followups.a: Without it, clients that failed together retry together, in waves. Random jitter spreads the retries over time so the dependency sees a smooth trickle instead of spikes.

followups.q: Circuit breaker vs retry: which goes outside?
followups.a: Usually the breaker wraps the retries' attempts or sits at the same layer, so when it is open no retries happen at all. Retries handle short blips; the breaker handles longer outages.
A separate limit of threads or concurrent calls per dependency, like watertight compartments in a ship. If one engine hangs, only its compartment fills; calls to other engines still run.

followups.q: How does Envoy outlier detection differ?
followups.a: It works per host inside a cluster: after 5 consecutive 5xx errors by default it ejects that host for a while, longer each time, while healthy hosts keep serving.

check.q: The breaker's wait timer has ended. What happens next?
check.a: A few trial calls are let through (half-open)
d: All traffic flows again at once
It stays open until restarted by hand
It retries every queued call immediately
check.why: Half-open lets a small number of probes test the dependency before trusting it fully.

check.q: Five layers each retry 3 times during an outage. What happens to the bottom service?
check.a: Its load is multiplied many times over
d: The retries cancel each other out
check.why: Retries multiply per layer (3 to the power 5 gives 243x), which is why you retry at one layer only.

check.q: Why set a minimum number of calls before the breaker can trip?
check.a: So a few errors on low traffic do not open it
check.why: Two failures out of three calls is 66%, but it says little. The minimum makes the rate meaningful.

check.q: Which retry pattern spreads clients out best?
check.why: Jitter adds randomness so clients that failed together do not retry in the same instant.
